title: The Pratfall Effect

scenes.text: Spilling coffee might make you *more* likeable.
scenes.vo: Spilling coffee on yourself might actually make people like you more.
In 1966, psychologist Elliot Aronson played people a recording of a quiz-show contestant.

scenes.text:
A near-perfect contestant…
then spills coffee on himself
scenes.vo: The contestant got almost every answer right. In one version, he then clumsily spilled coffee all over himself.

scenes.text:
The clumsy expert was rated
*more* likeable
scenes.vo: Listeners rated the clumsy expert as more likeable than the flawless one.

scenes.text: But only if he was already *competent*
scenes.vo: But here's the catch: when the contestant was average, the same blunder made him less likeable.
This is the pratfall effect. A small flaw makes competent people feel human and relatable.

scenes.text: Good at your job? Owning a small mistake builds *trust*.
scenes.vo: So if you're good at what you do, owning a small mistake builds trust, not doubt.

caption:
Perfect is intimidating. A little imperfection makes skill relatable. ☕

Do you trust people more when they admit a mistake? 👇
source: Aronson, E., Willerman, B. & Floyd, J. (1966). The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness. Psychonomic Science, 4(6).
